titulo: Two kisses, one hand, and knowing when to go
subtitulo: The greeting that is settled by whoever moves first, the hand on your arm that means the evening is going well, the two seconds of quiet that mean you have found the edge of something, and the goodbye that runs on from the room to the street because it is meant to
cena: Half eleven at night, the plates went an hour ago, you have twice said you ought to be going, and the man beside you has just put a hand on your arm and started another story.
decisao: whether you stay when the room means stay and go when it means go — the hour a table only opens after the food has gone, against the evening that ends at ten with everybody being very polite about it
frasePiso: You will know when the room wants you to stay and when it has finished, and be right about both. Most visitors go home at ten and never find out that the good hour comes after the plates.
permissao: You are allowed to put a hand out instead of a cheek, anywhere, with anybody, and nobody in Spain is offended by it — ever. You are allowed to go over the top of somebody who is still talking: no gap is coming, and holding out for one is how a visitor spends a whole evening silent. You are allowed to stay after the plates have gone, because the table is yours until somebody stands up. And you are allowed to say nothing at all for ten minutes at a loud table — nobody is counting your turns.
espelho: Backing off half a step when somebody moves in to talk to you is the bit that reads as odd there. Eighty centimetres of clear air is not respect at that table — it is read as somebody with somewhere else to be.

fichasCulturais.sinal: She comes across the room, tilts her head and goes for your right cheek before either of you has said a word.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have to do this now, I am going to pick the wrong side, and everybody is watching me pick it.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Two kisses are private rather than commercial: right cheek first, then left, and the lips land on nothing. Whoever puts a hand out first has settled it for both of you, and the other person simply takes the hand.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Lean in, right cheek first, two words while it happens — or put your own hand out first and let that be the version.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The first three seconds stop being a negotiation, and you spend the rest of the evening talking instead of watching everybody's shoulders.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not across a counter, a desk or a till. Nobody selling you something, serving you or checking you in will offer it, and there the hand is the whole of the protocol.

fichasCulturais.sinal: He is standing closer than feels normal, he has not once dropped your eye, and a hand lands on your arm halfway through a sentence.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: This is a lot of person at close range, and I ought to give him a bit more room.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The arm is the thermometer of the conversation. It turns up when the thing is going well, and it is doing the work that a nod and an mm-hm do at home.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay exactly where you are, keep your eyes up, and carry on with what you were saying.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get read as present rather than as polite, the conversation keeps its temperature, and you get the second half of it — which is the half worth having.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a bank counter, at a doctor's, or with anybody in a uniform. Those keep about the distance yours does at home, and closeness there would be as odd for them as it is for you.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The table goes quiet for about two seconds and somebody starts a completely different subject without looking at you while they do it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I have offended them, and I need to explain what I actually meant before this gets any worse.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: That pause is the room drawing a line and then papering over it. The new subject is the repair, offered by somebody else precisely so that nobody has to name what happened.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Take the new subject at once, with interest, and leave the old one exactly where it fell.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: The evening carries on at the temperature it had, and you become the visitor who noticed — which is worth more than the story you were in the middle of.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not between them. They will go back over the same subject with each other for an hour, at volume. The two seconds are about who said it, not about what was said.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You put Thursday to somebody and what comes back is warm, agreeable and has no day of the week anywhere in it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That is a yes, then. He is going to message me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Ya te diré and ya veremos are the polite shape of no. They exist so that nobody has to hand somebody a flat one to their face, and everyone at the table hears them correctly.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Say vale, otro día, and change the subject yourself before he has to.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You keep the person, and the invitation they do mean still turns up later in the week.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not from a shop or an office, where ya le digo algo can be a real answer that is genuinely pending. This is about a plan between people, not about a quote for a job.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Midnight, everything has been cleared, no bill has come, and the moment you stand up three people ask whether you are off already.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: The evening finished half an hour ago and they are too well brought up to say so.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Clearing is not closing. The end is done with a body rather than a sentence: the host stands, says bueno, pues nada, and starts moving plates — and even then the goodbye itself runs on through the room, the hall and the street.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Sit back down once, stay another half hour, and leave when somebody else is on their feet.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the hour that only opens after the food has gone, which is the hour where you stop being the guest and start being the person they ask back.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a restaurant on its last sitting, where chairs going up on tables is exactly what it looks like — and not on a weeknight in a house with school in the morning.

Pe-ro, never perrro. The finger flicks off your leg once and stops dead. Three more, out loud.

steps.promptPt: Last night's street, the band long gone by, and the woman beside you still has not moved an inch. Ask her what the day is. Speak now.
steps.pt: four words, to whoever is nearest
That was them out in the street. Tonight is the other end of it, a metre away from your face.
Half eleven, the plates went an hour ago, and you have twice said you ought to be going.

Three things get said to you tonight without one word in them. Stay. Ease off. And now you can go.
The first one you send yourself, at the door, out loud, before anybody in there has looked up.
One word, any hour of the day. Shop, bar, lift, waiting room — it is the entrance fee.

steps.promptPt: You have pushed open the door of a small bar with four people in it, and every one of them has looked up at you. One word, from the doorway. Speak now.
steps.pt: before anything else happens
Silence in a doorway reads as coldness there. One word buys you the room for the next hour.
Then the greeting itself, and it is the bit that puts British visitors on the back foot.
Two kisses. Right cheek first, then the left, and the lips land on nothing at all.
It is private, not commercial. Nobody at a counter, a desk or a till is going to do it.
And the hand settles it. Whoever puts one out has chosen, and the other person takes it.
Put yours out and nobody in Spain is offended. Ever. That is the whole of the get-out.
Pleased to meet you. — two words that go with either version, and they never change shape.

steps.promptPt: A friend of a friend has walked into the flat, come straight across the room and is already leaning in. Two words, while it is happening. Speak now.
steps.pt: two words, whichever way it goes
👂 What comes back at you. Take it by ear — yours is already said and it fits anybody.
Now the thing that is not a rule at all. It is a distance, and it is shorter than the one you keep.
Round that table the gap is smaller, the eyes stay on you, and a hand lands on your arm mid-sentence.
That hand is the welcome. It shows up once the conversation is going well, and never before.
Take half a step back and the temperature changes, and neither of you can say quite why.
So the body action tonight is nothing. Stay put, eyes up, and let the arm happen.
GUIRI ALERT. George here. Woman at a barbecue leaned in, and I put my hand out like a bank manager.
She took it, shook it, and the whole table watched me arrange a mortgage with her mother.
Nobody minded that. What they did clock was me reversing half a metre afterwards.
The volume works the same way. Four people going at once is not a row. It is interest.
Nobody is holding a gap open for you, because a gap means the subject has died on the table.
Listen — one thing. Three words that take the floor without anybody being interrupted.
Say it at normal speed, straight across whoever is going, and the table turns round to you.

steps.promptPt: Five of them round a table, all going at once, no pause in six minutes, and you have something to add. Over the top of him. Speak now.
steps.pt: three words, and the table turns
And when the whole thing runs off without you, there is a line you have owned since week one.
The sentence that keeps a table where it was, once somebody has switched over for you.

steps.promptPt: You get to the table and the whole lot of them switch into English mid-sentence, purely out of kindness. Hand it back to them. Speak now.
steps.pt: and the table comes back
It is not a correction of them. It says you would rather work at it, and most of them will.
Now the second signal, and it lasts about two seconds. The table goes quiet all at once.
Somebody starts a completely different subject, and nobody looks at you while they do it.
That is the room telling you where the edge was. It is not anger, and it is already over.
What you do is take the new subject, at once, and leave the old one where it fell.
An apology reopens it. The two seconds close it, and everybody at that table would rather they did.
👂 Flat, short, eyes elsewhere — the same two seconds, in words. Move on with them.
The same flatness turns up in an answer that sounds like a yes and is nothing of the kind.
👂 I'll let you know. Nobody is going to let you know. It is a no with the door left open.
👂 We'll see. The same answer in a different coat. Neither of them is a plan.
Chase either one and you make somebody say a word they were being kind by leaving out.
All right, another day. Three words that let somebody off without anybody losing face.

steps.promptPt: You have put Thursday to him twice now, and what comes back is warm, agreeable and pins nothing down. Let him off it. Speak now.
steps.pt: and nobody has to say it out loud
Say that, and the invitation they do mean still turns up. Push once more and it quietly stops.
One word you will overhear about yourself, and it lands nothing like it sounds.
👂 Look — the guiris. Northern-European visitor. Teasing, rarely hostile, and not a shot at you.
It names a category, not a person, and there is normally no hostility in it, often the opposite.
Last signal, and it is the one British visitors read four hours early, every single time.
The plates going does not mean it. No bill coming does not mean it either — that is the rule.
A quiet minute does not mean it. Somebody on a phone for two minutes does not mean it.
👂 Off already? Asked at midnight, of somebody who stood up two hours early.
That is not a formality either. It is the table asking you to sit back down again.

steps.es: No, no, me quedo un rato.

steps.es: No, no, me quedo un rato.

The host stands up and starts moving plates about. That is the end of it, and the only one.

steps.promptPt: The door of the flat, coats on, and the woman whose kitchen it was has both hands out for you. Two words. Speak now.
steps.pt: two words, at the door
That is the room. Stay put, go over the top, let the two seconds pass, and leave last. Hasta luego.

aprofundar.titulo: The greeting, the arm, the two seconds and the long goodbye (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Two kisses, one hand, and why neither of them is a rule
secoes.corpo: The shape is simple and it is worth having in your head before you need it: two kisses, right cheek to right cheek first, then the left, cheeks touching or nearly touching and the lips landing on nothing. It is the private greeting — friends, family, a friend of a friend, somebody's flat, an introduction at a table — and it runs between women, and between a woman and a man. Two men who are not family shake hands, or do the hand-plus-shoulder version if they know each other well. What it is not is commercial: nobody behind a counter, a desk, a till or a hotel reception is going to offer it, and if you go in for it there you have simply misread which kind of room you are in. The piece that makes all of this manageable is that the hand settles it. Whoever puts a hand out first has chosen for both people, and the other person takes the hand without a flicker. So the get-out is total and you should use it whenever you want to: put your hand out, and nobody in Spain is offended, ever. One honest note on where this comes from. This is a description of a well-attested convention, not a measured finding — the best European observational work on greeting distance and touch does not include Spain at all, so anybody telling you that studies show Spaniards stand exactly so many centimetres closer is inventing the precision. What you have here is the behaviour and the way out of it, which is all you need at a door.

exemplos.pt: MOO-choh GOOS-toh — pleased to meet you. Fits the hand and fits the cheeks, and never changes shape
en-kahn-TAH-dhoh — 👂 the one that comes back at you. Recognise it; you do not need to produce it

secoes.titulo: Closer, louder, and over the top
secoes.corpo: Three things about a Spanish table read to a British ear as something they are not. The distance is shorter, the volume is higher, and people talk on top of each other. None of the three is aggression, and the third one is the one that costs visitors the most, because the British conversational habit is to wait for a gap that is never going to open. A gap in that conversation does not mean 'your turn' — it means the subject has died, and somebody will now change it. The way in is to go over the top at ordinary volume, and there is a set of little openers for doing exactly that: 'oye', 'oye, una cosa', 'pues yo…', 'mira'. They are not rude and they are not clever; they are the ordinary machinery of taking a turn. The hand on the arm belongs to the same family. It arrives when the conversation is going well, it is a marker of engagement rather than of intimacy, and the single most useful thing you can do with it is nothing at all: stay where you are. Stepping back is a reply, whether you meant it as one or not, and it is read as wanting to be elsewhere. And on volume, one permission worth repeating from the first week: talking a bit louder than feels polite to you is what gets you heard, and lowering your voice in a loud bar is the thing that marks you out.

exemplos.pt: OH-yeh, OO-nah KOH-sah — listen, one thing. The floor, taken without a gap
pwehs yoh KREH-oh keh — 👂 well I reckon… The other standard way in, over the top of somebody

secoes.titulo: The two seconds, and the no that never gets said
secoes.corpo: Every room has an edge somewhere, and the way this one tells you that you have found it is a two-second silence followed by somebody starting a different subject and not looking at you while they do it. It is not anger, it is not a sanction, and it is finished by the time you have noticed it — the new subject is the repair, and it has been offered by somebody else so that nobody has to say what happened. The correct move is therefore the cheapest one available: take the new subject with interest and leave the old one lying there. An apology reopens the thing you were being let off, and now everybody has to have the conversation nobody wanted. The flat 'ya, ya' with the eyes elsewhere is the spoken version of the same two seconds. The near relative of all this is the refusal that is not phrased as one. 'Ya te diré' — I'll let you know — and 'ya veremos' — we'll see — are polite noes, and 'es complicado' is a third. None of them is a plan, and pressing for a date turns a comfortable no into an uncomfortable one that somebody now has to say to your face. 'Vale, otro día' releases them, keeps the friendship intact, and keeps you on the list for the invitation they actually do mean. The one place to be careful with this reading is commercial: 'ya le digo algo' from a workshop or an office can be a genuinely pending answer, and there it is fair to ring back.

exemplos.pt: yah teh dee-REH — 👂 I'll let you know / we'll see. Both are no, said kindly
BAH-leh, OH-troh DEE-ah — all right, another day. The answer that keeps everybody

secoes.titulo: Guiri, and what the word is actually pointing at
secoes.corpo: You will hear it, probably in the third person and probably not aimed at you: guiri, the ordinary slang word for a northern-European visitor. It is teasing and it is usually fond; it is not an insult, and it is not a word anybody is going to use to your face as an attack. What it points at is not your nationality but a set of visible habits — the eleven-in-the-morning beer, the shirt off two streets from the sand, the socks and sandals, the sunburn, the wallet on the table. Which is the useful bit: it is a description of behaviour, and behaviour is adjustable in a way that a passport is not. Two things follow. First, hearing it is information rather than hostility, and reacting to it as an insult is itself the most guiri thing available in the moment. Second, the same word is doing a job for them that no English word quite does, halfway between 'tourist' and 'holidaymaker', and it is used about the whole category with a certain affection — the guiri, after all, is also the person paying for the terrace. Whether you make a joke of it about yourself is a separate skill, and it lives in a part of its own.

exemplos.pt: MEE-rah, lohs GEE-rees — 👂 look, the guiris. Overheard, not aimed
SOH-mohs GEE-rees — 👂 we're guiris, we know. The shape it takes when it is said with a laugh

secoes.titulo: Leaving: the signal that starts it, and the twenty minutes after
secoes.corpo: The British reading of 'the evening is over' is built out of things that mean nothing here. The plates being cleared means the food has finished, not the evening — the hour after the plates is the sobremesa, and in a lot of houses it is the best hour of the night. The bill not arriving means the table is still yours, because bringing it unasked is read as throwing a customer out. A quiet minute means somebody is thinking. What actually ends it is physical and it is unmistakable once you know to look for it: the host gets to their feet, says something like 'bueno, pues nada', and starts moving plates or glasses. Before that, standing up gets you '¿ya te vas?', which is not a formality — it is an invitation to sit down again, and 'no, no, me quedo un rato' is the whole of the answer. After it, the leaving itself is a process rather than a moment: goodbyes in the room, more in the hall, more at the door, and a last one from the street, and it genuinely runs on for a good ten minutes. This is not politeness theatre to be escaped; it is the part where the invitation to come back gets made. The way to get it wrong in the other direction is to make the announcement and then keep sitting there, which reads as wanting to be persuaded. Announce it on your feet, with the jacket in your hand, and mean it — and then let the twenty minutes happen.

exemplos.pt: yah teh bahs — 👂 off already? An invitation to sit back down, not a question
BWEH-noh, pwehs NAH-dhah — 👂 right then, that's that. Said standing. This one is the real signal
